text.en:
Gopal watched a goldsmith beat a small piece of gold into a thin sheet and pull another piece into a fine wire.
"Why does gold not break?" he asked. "Because metals are malleable and ductile," the goldsmith said.

Metals are usually hard, shiny (lustrous) and good conductors of heat and electricity. They can be beaten into thin sheets (malleable) and drawn into wires (ductile). Many metals make a ringing sound when struck (sonorous). Examples are iron, copper, aluminium, gold and silver.
Non-metals such as carbon, sulphur, oxygen and nitrogen are usually dull, soft or brittle and are poor conductors. Many are gases.
Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature. Graphite, a form of carbon, conducts electricity even though carbon is a non-metal. Metals are used for wires, vessels and tools; non-metals are used for fuels, fertilisers and more.
Metals are shiny and hard. They conduct heat and electricity.
Metals can be beaten into sheets and drawn into wires. They make a ringing sound.
Non-metals are usually dull and poor conductors. Many are gases.
Mercury is a liquid metal. Graphite is a non-metal that conducts.

problem.en: Why are electric wires made of copper and covered with plastic?

text.en: Copper is a good conductor and ductile, so it is drawn into wires.
Plastic is an insulator, so it keeps the current from escaping.
So the wire carries current safely.

why.en: Each material is chosen for its property.

prompt.en: A friend says all non-metals are gases. How will you correct this?

requiredIdeas.en: Carbon and sulphur are solid non-metals.

points.en: Metals are shiny, hard, malleable, ductile and conduct.
Non-metals are usually dull and poor conductors.
There are exceptions: mercury and graphite.
